title: Integration middleware: how to connect your product to customers' systems of record (2026)
summary: How in-house builds, iPaaS, embedded iPaaS, and unified APIs compare on scalability, maintenance, and tech debt for customer-facing integrations.
body_markdown:
Building the first integration has become straightforward with the recent progress in AI, but complexity can quickly compound the more systems you add. Every system added becomes yours to maintain, and customers onboard often bring new edge cases to fix.


Integration middleware promises to remove that burden for you, so you can focus on your core product. The different providers differ most in architecture, who writes each system’s integration logic, and who owns the maintenance. The following article aims to provide an overview of this.


**Key takeaways (October 26, 2026)**


- Integration middleware covers two distinct use cases: internal, which connects systems your company owns, and customer-facing, which connects your product to systems your customers own. Any software vendor whose product depends on customer data needs the second.
- For customer-facing integrations, the six options are building in-house, enterprise iPaaS, embedded iPaaS, code-first integration platforms, unified APIs, and standards or file exchange. They differ on where per-system logic lives, which data model you build against, and what grows when you add a customer. ESBs, message brokers, and API management serve a company’s own systems.
- On an iPaaS, work typically scales linearly with connected customers, because each one gets its own workflow. With a unified API, work grows with every system, and the provider does it once for all customers.


## What is integration middleware?


Integration middleware is software that sits between systems and moves, translates, and routes data between them. Instead of calling each system’s API directly, your product integrates with the middleware, which then abstracts the rest.


For a software vendor, that’s the layer between your product and each customer’s systems of record. A system of record is the authoritative source for one type of business data, for example:


- **HRIS:** employees and org structure
- **ATS:** candidates and applications
- **Payroll:** pay and deductions
- **LMS:** courses and learning records
- **ERP and CRM:** finance and customer data


### Internal vs customer-facing integration middleware


There are two kinds of integration middleware, and they solve different problems. Internal middleware connects internal systems owned by one company. Customer-facing middleware connects your product to systems your customers use.


Internal and customer-facing integration middleware Internal integration middleware Customer-facing integration middleware


Example Your HR team syncs your own Workday data with your reporting dashboards Your assessment product writes scores into each customer’s Greenhouse, Workday Recruiting, or iCIMS


Who owns the connected systems You Your customers


Number of instances One per system pair One per customer, often hundreds


Who typically configures it Your IT or ops team Your customer’s admin, through your product


What happens when it breaks An internal process stalls Your product breaks for a customer


Typical tools Workato, MuleSoft, Boomi Unified APIs (Kombo, Merge, Finch), embedded iPaaS (Paragon, Prismatic, Tray Embedded)


## What are the options for connecting your product to customers’ systems of record?


Software vendors have six ways to connect to customers’ systems of record: build in-house, use an enterprise iPaaS, use an embedded iPaaS, use a code-first integration platform, use a unified API, or rely on standards and file exchange. They differ mainly in who writes and maintains the logic for each system, and how scalable they are.


### Why use integration middleware: scalability, maintenance, and tech debt


Teams typically adopt integration middleware for three reasons:


- **Scalability:** Every new system of record and every new customer adds integration work.
- **Maintenance:** Integration work (unfortunately) doesn’t end afther they’re built. APIs get versioned and deprecated, credentials expire, or hit rate limits. Someone has to notice and fix each break, often while a customer is waiting.
- **Tech debt.** Every integration you own adds code, mappings, and edge cases that have nothing to do with your core product.


The options below split these costs between your team and the provider in different ways, whilen the comparison table at the end of this section shows how.


### Building integrations in-house


**What it is:** Your engineers write and maintain a direct integration to each system’s API.


**Examples:** An integration with Ashby or BambooHR


**Best for:** One or two (simpler) systems that are central to your product, where you need full control and have engineers to spare.


**Where it breaks:** Cost grows with every system you add. Based on what Kombo hears from customers, teams spend about 80 engineering hours per production-grade integration (not counting maintenance). The benefits platform Ben built its BambooHR and Workday integrations in-house before concluding that integration work shouldn’t be core to its product ([Ben case study](https://www.kombo.dev/case-study/ben) ).


### Enterprise iPaaS (Workato, MuleSoft, Boomi)


**What it is:** A platform for building automated workflows, called recipes or flows, between applications, run by IT for internal processes.


**Examples:**[Workato](https://www.workato.com/) ,[MuleSoft](https://www.mulesoft.com/) ,[Boomi](https://boomi.com/)


**Best for:** Connecting the systems your own company runs, with complex internal routing and approvals.


**Where it breaks:** Every customer needs its own connection, credentials, and field mapping, and your team maintains each one as a separate workflow. This slows down onboarding and creates a growing maintenance debt.


### Embedded iPaaS (Paragon, Prismatic, Tray Embedded, Workato Embedded)


**What it is:** An iPaaS you embed in your product, so customers connect their accounts and run integrations you built on the platform.


**Examples:**[Workato Embedded](https://docs.workato.com/en/oem/workato-embedded.html) ,[Tray Embedded](https://tray.ai/solutions/by-use-case/embedded-integration/) ,[Prismatic](https://prismatic.io/platform/embedded-workflow-builder/) ,[Paragon](https://www.useparagon.com/connect-portal)


**Best for:** Products whose customers want to configure their own workflows across many app categories, especially CRM, support tools, and messaging.


**Where it breaks:** You still write the domain logic for each system on top of the platform’s connectors, including how to create a Workday worker or read SAP SuccessFactors employment data.[Tray.ai’s guide](https://tray.ai/embedded) states the issue with this - when each customer gets a copy with their own tweaks, “one fix has to be made four hundred times.”


### Code-first integration platforms (Nango, Ampersand)


**What it is:** Managed infrastructure for authentication, syncs, and webhooks, where your engineers define each integration in code or declarative config against the system’s native objects.


**Examples:**[Nango](https://www.nango.dev/) ,[Ampersand](https://www.ampersand.ai/)


**Best for:** Engineering teams that want native data models and full control over each integration, without running auth and sync infrastructure themselves.


**Where it breaks:** You still own the logic and maintenance for each system, so every new system is a new build for your team.


### Unified API (Kombo, Merge, Finch,[Unified.to](http://unified.to/) , Apideck)


**What it is:** One normalized API for a whole category, such as HRIS or ATS. The provider builds and maintains the integration for each system behind it.


**Examples:**


- [Kombo](https://www.kombo.dev/integrations) covers HRIS, payroll, ATS, assessment, and LMS.
- [Finch](https://www.tryfinch.com/finch-api) describes itself as “the unified API for payroll, HR, and benefits.”
- [Unified.to](https://unified.to/) runs real-time pass-through requests across 37 categories.
- [Apideck’s HRIS API](https://www.apideck.com/hris-api) listed 60 connectors when checked on October 19, 2026.
- [Merge](https://docs.merge.dev/hris/overview/) offers HRIS alongside seven other categories, including CRM, accounting, and ticketing.


**Best for:** Products that read and write the same kind of data, such as employees, candidates, or courses, for many customers across many systems.


**Where it breaks:** When the normalized model is missing a field or action you need, you usually have to write the code yourself per integration. Check coverage, field mapping and transformation capabilities, and developer tooling across systems before you commit.


### Standards and file exchange (LTI, xAPI, SCORM, SFTP)


**What it is:** Agreed formats rather than vendor APIs.[LTI 1.3](https://www.1edtech.org/standards/lti) from 1EdTech connects learning tools to an institution’s learning platform, with grade passback through Assignment and Grade Services. SCORM and xAPI, both developed by the[ADL Initiative](https://adlnet.gov/) , package learning content and record learning activity. SFTP exchanges scheduled flat files, which many enterprise payroll setups still use.


**Best for:** Launching content inside academic LMSs like Canvas or D2L. SFTP fits payroll and HRIS setups that only expose file interfaces.


**Where it breaks:** LTI covers launch and grades inside an institution’s LMS, not HR data like users, org structures, or skills. SFTP files run on a schedule, and the file layout often differs from one customer to the next.


### Integration middleware comparison table


Integration middleware options compared In-house Enterprise iPaaS Embedded iPaaS Code-first platform Unified API Standards & files


Who maintains per-system logic Your engineers Your team, per workflow Your team, on vendor connectors Your engineers, on vendor auth and sync infrastructure The unified API provider The standard; you implement it


Data model Yours Each app’s native model Each app’s native model Each system’s native model, or one you define Normalized, plus raw data and passthrough Defined by the standard or file spec


Write support Whatever you build Whatever you build per recipe Whatever you build per integration Whatever you build Per provider and per system; check the coverage tables Limited to the standard (e.g. LTI grades)


Customer onboarding You build auth and setup Not designed for end customers Embedded connect UI Embedded connect UI Embedded connect flow Manual setup per customer


Maintenance burden High, grows with each system High, grows with each customer Medium, grows with each system Medium, grows with each system Low for you; the provider absorbs API changes Low, but file layouts drift per customer


How it scales Linearly with systems, engineering headcount is the limit Linearly with customers, one workflow per customer With systems, plus drift as customer-specific edits accumulate With systems; each new system is a build for your team New systems and customers cost your team little With customers, each file feed or LTI setup is configured separately


Tech debt you take on API clients, mappings, retries, customer workarounds Workflow sprawl, often owned outside engineering Integration logic on a vendor platform, hard to move off Integration code per system One integration, plus provider dependence to weigh File parsers and per-customer mappings


Best for 1–2 core systems Internal IT workflows Customer-configured workflows across categories Integrations core to your product, with engineers to own them Productized ATS, HRIS, payroll, and LMS integrations at scale Academic LMS content, file-only payroll


## How integration middleware architectures differ


Integration middleware architectures differ on where each system’s integration logic lives (most decisise for your long-term costs), which data model your product codes against, how data is synced and stored, how each customer’s credentials are handled, and how writes are validated.


### Where per-system logic lives, and what grows with each customer


Every system brings its own logic around authentication, endpoints, pagination, field mapping, rate limits, and the quirks of each customer’s tenant. Here’s a breakdown of what this means across middleware architectures:


Where per-system integration logic lives Architecture Where per-system logic lives Adding a customer means Adding a system means


In-house Your codebase, one integration per system Configuration, sometimes custom code A new build for your team


Enterprise iPaaS Workflows on the platform, usually one per customer Cloning and editing a workflow New workflows for each customer on that system


Embedded iPaaS Your templates on the vendor’s connectors, deployed per customer Deploying an instance, plus any customer-specific edits A new template for your team


Code-first platform Your code, on the vendor’s auth and sync infrastructure The customer connecting an account A new build for your team


Unified API The provider’s connectors, shared across all its customers The customer connecting an account Nothing for your team, if the provider supports the system


### Native vs normalized data models


With native models, your product codes against each system’s own objects, such as a Workday worker, a SAP SuccessFactors employment record, or a Greenhouse application. You get full fidelity, but your product logic branches for every system.


With a normalized model, which is what unified APIs offer, your product codes against one standardized employee or application schema. The risk is a lowest-common-denominator model, so most providers offer one of multiple options across custom field mapping, field transformation, raw source data on each record, and passthrough requests to the source API.


### Sync and state: who detects changes


Middleware either fetches data when you ask for it (request-time) or keeps its own copy and syncs it (sync-and-store). Many systems of record, HRIS and ATS especially, offer no or unreliable webhooks, so detecting a new hire, a stage change, or a deleted record usually means polling and comparing snapshots.


Whoever holds the state does that work: your database (in-house and iPaaS), the provider (sync-and-store unified APIs), or your product again (pass-through). Polling also runs into each source system’s rate limits, which sync-and-store providers absorb and pass-through providers pass on to you.


Sync-and-store compared with pass-through Sync-and-store Pass-through (real-time)


How it works The provider syncs and caches data, then serves your reads from its copy Every request goes live to the source system


Examples Kombo, Merge ([sync frequency docs](https://docs.merge.dev/hris/overview/) ), Finch ([daily refresh by default](https://www.tryfinch.com/finch-api) )[Unified.to](http://unified.to/) ([real-time, zero-storage](https://unified.to/) ),[Apideck](https://www.apideck.com/hris-api)


Strengths Fast reads, change and deletion detection, webhooks on changes, fewer calls against source rate limits Data is never older than the source, and the provider stores no end-customer data


Trade-offs Data at rest widens compliance scope; freshness depends on sync interval Bound by each source’s rate limits and latency; detecting changes and deletions takes more work


Best for Products that react to changes (joiners and leavers, stage changes) Products that read small amounts of data on demand


### Writes, validation, and idempotency


Creating a hire in Workday or writing a result to an ATS has to pass each tenant’s required fields, picklist values, and business process rules, and some writes finish asynchronously, for example when a Workday business process needs approval. Good middleware validates before writing, returns system-specific errors you can show the customer, and makes retries idempotent, so a timeout doesn’t create a duplicate employee or application.


### Other middleware types: ESB, message brokers, API management, ETL, and RPA


Most lists of middleware types also include architectures built for a company’s own systems. They’re useful inside your own stack, but they don’t connect your product to your customers’ systems of record.


Other middleware types and why they rarely fit customer-facing products Type What it does Why it rarely fits customer-facing integrations


Enterprise service bus (ESB) Routes and transforms messages between a company’s own, often on-premise, systems through a central bus Heavy to run, and assumes you own every connected system


Message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ) Deliver events asynchronously between services Move events you already have; they don’t call Workday or Greenhouse for you


API management (Apigee, Kong) Secures, rate-limits, and meters APIs you expose Governs the APIs you publish, not the ones you consume


ETL and ELT (Fivetran, Airbyte) Copies data into a warehouse on a schedule One-way and built for analytics, not in-product reads and writes


Robotic process automation (UiPath) Bots operate a system’s user interface Breaks when the interface changes; a last resort for systems without an API


## Does MCP replace integration middleware for AI products?


No - MCP standardizes how an AI agent discovers and calls tools, but it doesn’t connect to your customers’ systems of record by itself. An MCP server for Workday or Greenhouse still needs per-customer authentication, a data model, change detection, and safe writes. For AI agents that act on customer data, such as recruiting, interviewing, or HR agents, MCP is the interface the agent uses, and integration middleware sits behind it. The non-deterministic nature of MCP also makes it a poor fit for many operations writing back to system of records.


## Integration middleware by system of record


The architecture choice plays out differently for each system of record, because each holds different data and breaks in different places. The sections below cover three common ones: the ATS, the HRIS and payroll system, and the corporate LMS.


## What is the best integration middleware for ATS integrations?


For hiring products that write back to many customers’ ATSs, a unified API with per-system write coverage fits best. An embedded iPaaS can work if your customers use only one or two mid-market ATSs. As of October 26, 2026, Kombo supports 108 ATS and 18 assessment and background-check integrations. It posts applications on 103 ATS integrations, moves applications to a new stage on 52, and posts screening-question answers on 56. Kombo is a certified Greenhouse partner \[VERIFY: link to Kombo’s Greenhouse Partner Directory listing\].


**Typical data flows:**


- Read jobs, candidates, applications, and interview stages.
- Create candidates and applications from job boards, sourcing tools, or careers pages.
- Move applications between stages, or reject with a note.
- Write assessment results and result links back to the candidate.


**Where it gets hard:** Writes. Fewer providers can update stages, upload attachments, or post assessment results, because each ATS exposes these differently or only to certified partners. Enterprise tenants add variation: two Workday Recruiting, SAP SuccessFactors, or Oracle Recruiting Cloud customers can have different stages, required fields, and screening questions. Ask for write coverage per system, not per category. See[the best unified APIs for ATS integrations](https://www.kombo.dev/blog/best-unified-api-ats-integrations) .


## What is the best integration middleware for HRIS and payroll integrations?


For onboarding, benefits, workforce planning, and identity products, a unified API with enterprise depth and per-system write coverage fits best. As of October 26, 2026, Kombo supports 85 API-based HRIS and payroll integrations. It creates employees on 36, writes absences on 34, and reads payslips and pay runs on Workday, UKG Pro, UKG Ready, and Dayforce. It holds certified partnerships with Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle, and UKG.


**Typical data flows:**


- Read employees, employments, org structure, and compensation.
- Detect joiners, movers, and leavers.
- Create employees and absences.
- Read payroll data, or write benefit deductions.


**Where it gets hard:** Workday data often sits in customer-built custom reports (RaaS), so Workday needs separate paths for the API, custom reports, and SFTP delivery. Kombo runs three[Workday connectors](https://docs.kombo.dev/hris/connectors) for that reason. SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle HCM, and UKG Pro vary heavily by tenant. Payroll writes are the rarest: Finch supports deduction and contribution write-back today ([Finch API](https://www.tryfinch.com/finch-api) ), and Kombo’s payroll write is on its roadmap for Q4 2026. See[the best unified APIs for HRIS integrations](https://www.kombo.dev/blog/best-unified-api-hris-integrations) .


## What is the best integration middleware for corporate LMS integrations?


For corporate learning products, a unified LMS API fits best, ideally from a provider that also covers HRIS so you can pull org structure and managers alongside learning data. As of October 26, 2026, Kombo’s LMS API connects to 10 platforms: 360Learning, Cornerstone OnDemand, Coursera, Docebo, LinkedIn Learning, Moodle, SAP SuccessFactors Learning, TalentLMS, Udemy Business, and Workday Learning. That’s a different job from LTI, which launches content inside schools’ and universities’ learning platforms.


**Typical data flows:**


- Push your course catalog into the customer’s LMS.
- Enroll employees in courses, for example after a skills assessment.
- Write completions and scores back for compliance and L&D reporting.
- Read skills data to personalize learning paths.


**Where it gets hard:** Most LMSs expose users and courses, but fewer support enrollments, completions, or course upserts through the API. Some process writes asynchronously: Coursera can take up to 48 hours to show new enrollments ([Kombo LMS connectors](https://docs.kombo.dev/lms/connectors) ). Kombo’s per-system LMS coverage is listed under “Where Kombo fits” below.


## Why do Workato recipes break for customer-facing integrations?


An iPaaS like Workato breaks down once each customer needs its own workflow. Take a product that creates employees in each customer’s Workday through Workato. The first customer’s recipe maps your fields to their Hire Employee business process. The second customer has a different supervisory organization structure and two extra required fields, so the recipe gets cloned and edited. By customer twenty, there are twenty recipes, and a change to Workday’s API or to one customer’s business process means checking every copy.


**What scales better:** Keep the iPaaS for internal workflows and one-off custom logic. Move repeatable per-system work, like creating Workday employees or writing ATS results, to a unified API, where the provider maintains it once for every customer.


## How to evaluate integration middleware for systems of record: a checklist


To evaluate integration middleware for systems of record, check how much of each system is actually supported, read and write, for the systems your customers use. Then look at how failures get detected and fixed.


1. **Coverage:** Ask for the list of systems your pipeline uses, including Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle, UKG, iCIMS, and ADP.
2. **Data model depth and write actions:** Check write coverage for each system: create employee, update application stage, write assessment results, enroll in a course.
3. **Custom fields:** Enterprise customers keep critical data in custom fields. Ask whether you can map custom fields into the normalized model, transform values, and reach raw data through passthrough.
4. **Sync approach:** Decide between sync-and-store and pass-through (see “Sync and state” above), and ask how deletions and changes are detected.
5. **Auth and onboarding:** Look for an embedded, white-labeled connection flow and setup guides for each system that your customers’ admins can follow without your engineers.
6. **Observability:** Look for searchable logs per request, sync status per linked account, error webhooks, and log retention long enough to debug a customer complaint.
7. **Who fixes broken integrations:** Ask who gets paged when a customer’s Workday credentials expire or an API changes, and whether you get a direct line to engineers.
8. **Security and compliance:** Check for SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, GDPR, data residency (US, EU, and others), scopes that limit which fields are synced, and audit logs.
9. **Pricing model:** Compare per-connection, per-API-call, and platform-fee models against your expected number of connected customers.


## Build vs buy: what does an in-house integration cost?


An in-house HRIS integration takes about 120 engineering hours to build on average, not counting maintenance, based on what we heard from customers ([Kombo blog](https://www.kombo.dev/blog/forward-thinking-ats-platforms-do-more-than-hire-they-automate-onboarding) ). Multiply that by the number of systems in your pipeline, and then add upkeep for every API change and every customer-specific configuration.


To estimate your own build cost:


1. List the systems of record behind your open deals and current customers.
2. Multiply that count by about 80 engineering hours per HRIS integration, and the associated developer costs. Enterprise systems like Workday or SAP SuccessFactors usually take longer.
3. Add maintenance: API version changes, credential expiry, and per-customer custom fields.
4. Add the time to get test access. For Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, and Oracle, that usually takes a partnership.


On the buy side, compare providers on time to the first live integration, how pricing scales with connected customers (per connection, per API call, or platform fee), and who absorbs maintenance when a system’s API or a customer’s setup changes.

## Summary: choosing integration middleware


Choose integration middleware by who owns the systems of record. For your own systems, an enterprise iPaaS works. For your customers’ systems of record, such as their HRIS, ATS, payroll, or corporate LMS, a unified API takes the per-system work off your team. Check write coverage and custom-field support against the systems in your pipeline. To test this on your own customers’ systems,[start a free proof of concept with Kombo](https://www.kombo.dev/pricing) or browse[Kombo’s integrations](https://www.kombo.dev/integrations) .


## Frequently asked questions


What is integration middleware?


+


Integration middleware is software that sits between systems and moves, translates, and routes data between them, so your product talks to the middleware instead of calling each system's API directly. For software vendors, it is the layer that connects a product to its customers' systems of record, such as their HRIS, ATS, payroll, or LMS. The common types for that job are embedded iPaaS, code-first integration platforms, and unified APIs.


What is a system of record?


+


A system of record is the authoritative source for one kind of business data inside a company: the HRIS for employees, the ATS for candidates, the payroll system for pay, the LMS for learning records, the ERP for finance. Software that depends on that data has to integrate with each customer's system of record, which is the job of customer-facing integration middleware.


What are the types of integration middleware?


+


For connecting a product to customers' systems of record, there are six options: in-house code, enterprise iPaaS, embedded iPaaS, code-first integration platforms, unified APIs, and standards or file exchange. Embedded iPaaS, code-first platforms, and unified APIs are built for one connection per customer. ESBs, message brokers, API management, ETL, and RPA serve a company's own systems.


What is the difference between integration middleware, iPaaS, and a unified API?


+


Integration middleware is the umbrella term. An iPaaS is middleware where you build workflows between apps, either for internal use (Workato, MuleSoft, Boomi) or embedded in your product (Paragon, Prismatic, Tray Embedded). A unified API, such as Kombo, Merge, or Finch, exposes one normalized API for a category like HRIS or ATS, and the provider maintains the integration for each system behind it. That means integration work grows with the number of systems, not the number of customers.


Is a unified API a type of middleware?


+


Yes. A unified API is customer-facing integration middleware that translates many systems' APIs into one data model. Kombo, for example, sits between a software product and each customer's HRIS, payroll, ATS, assessment, or LMS system, such as Workday, Greenhouse, or Cornerstone, and handles authentication, syncing, and writes for each one.


What is the best middleware for ATS integrations?


+


For a product that reads and writes candidates, applications, and assessment results across many customers' ATSs, a unified API with documented write coverage is usually the best fit. As of October 26, 2026, Kombo supports 108 ATS integrations, including Greenhouse, Lever, Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, iCIMS, and Oracle Recruiting Cloud. It posts applications on 103 of them, moves applications to a new stage on 52, and posts screening-question answers on 56. Compare write coverage for each system, since it varies by ATS.


What is the best middleware for HRIS integrations?


+


For products that sync employees and org data from many customers' HR systems, a unified API is usually the best fit. As of October 26, 2026, Kombo supports 85 API-based HRIS and payroll integrations, including Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle HCM, UKG Pro, and ADP Workforce Now. It creates employees on 36 and reads payslips and pay runs on Workday, UKG Pro, UKG Ready, and Dayforce. Check write coverage per system, such as creating employees, writing absences, or payroll deductions, since it varies by HRIS and by provider.


What is the best middleware for LMS integrations?


+


For corporate learning systems such as Cornerstone OnDemand, Docebo, Workday Learning, and SAP SuccessFactors Learning, a unified LMS API is usually the best fit, because it syncs users, courses, enrollments, completions, and skills through one schema. As of October 26, 2026, Kombo's LMS API connects to 10 platforms, including 360Learning, Coursera, LinkedIn Learning, Moodle, TalentLMS, and Udemy Business. Kombo covers LMS alongside HRIS, so learning products can pull org structure and managers through the same integration.


Is embedded iPaaS a good fit for HRIS integrations?


+


Embedded iPaaS fits when customers need to configure their own workflows and you only support a few HR systems. You still write each system's logic on top of the platform's connectors and maintain customer-specific copies, so work grows with every customer. For many HRIS behind one data model, a unified API such as Kombo takes that work off your team.


Should payroll integrations use SFTP files or APIs?


+


Use an API when the payroll system exposes the objects and write actions you need, because APIs allow faster updates and better error handling. Use SFTP when the payroll provider or the customer's setup only supports file exchange, which is still common in enterprise payroll. Kombo supports both API-based and SFTP-based HRIS and payroll integrations; SFTP connections aren't included in its count of API-based integrations.


How long does a Workday integration take to build in-house?


+


Based on what Kombo hears from customers, an HRIS integration takes about 120 engineering hours to build, not counting maintenance, and Workday usually takes longer. Workday tenants differ in business processes and custom reports, and test access usually requires a Workday partnership. Kombo is a certified Workday partner and maintains Workday HCM, Recruiting, and Learning integrations for its customers.


Is Workato a good fit for customer-facing integrations?


+


Workato fits internal workflows and products that need a few customer-specific automations. For customer-facing integrations at scale, each customer usually gets its own recipe, so a change in Workday or in a customer's business process has to be fixed in every copy. Teams that outgrow this move repeatable per-system work, like creating employees or writing ATS results, to a unified API such as Kombo, and keep Workato for internal and one-off logic.

Keep Workato for internal and one-off workflows.


Does MCP replace integration middleware?


+


No. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how an AI agent discovers and calls tools, but it doesn't connect to customers' systems of record by itself. An MCP server for Workday or Greenhouse still needs per-customer authentication, a data model, change detection, and safe writes, which is what integration middleware provides behind it.


What does an integration middleware engineer do?


+


An integration middleware engineer builds and maintains the connections between systems: authentication, data mapping, sync jobs, error handling, and monitoring. When a product integrates with customers' systems of record, that often means debugging customer-specific setups, such as a Workday or SAP SuccessFactors tenant, and keeping up with API changes. A unified API like Kombo moves much of that per-system work to the provider.
